```{r}
bw <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/bobwhite_counts.csv")
bad_fit <- lm(count ~ frac_built, data = bw)

nb_fit <- optim(par = c(mu0 = 12, b = -3, size = 1.4),
                fn = function(p){
                  mu <- p["mu0"] * exp(p["b"] * bw$frac_built)
                  -sum(dnbinom(bw$count, mu = mu, size = p["size"], log = TRUE))
                },
                method = "L-BFGS-B",
                lower = c(0.1, -20, 0.05), upper = c(100, 20, 50))
```

## The final project {.center}

## Three parts {.smaller}

| Part | Format | Builds on |
|---|---|---|
| **Code** | `.R` or `.Rmd`, or a GitHub link | every assignment so far |
| **Writing** | a document | your midterm Part 1 |
| **Presentation** | about 5 minutes | the whole thing |

. . .

**Due at the presentation**, during the scheduled final exam block.
Exact day and time to be confirmed.

::: {.notes}
Check the registrar's assigned exam slot before this class and fill in the date.
The course meets T/Th 2:00 to 3:50, which is not a pattern on the USF standard
matrix, so the slot is assigned rather than predictable. Finals week is Dec 5
to 10.

The design principle to state out loud: nothing here is new work. Every piece is
an extension of something they have already submitted and had feedback on.
:::

## Part 1: the code {.smaller}

A **full analysis**, not a fragment:

- loading the data
- any transformations, and the reason for them
- the code behind any modeling decision you made
- the model itself
- the figures

. . .

**Fully reproducible and well documented.** Someone else should be able to run
it and get your results.

::: {.notes}
"Reproducible" has a specific meaning here, and it is the one from Assignment 2:
someone else, on another machine, with your code and your data, gets your
numbers.

The most common failure is an absolute path to their own Desktop. The second is
data that only exists on their laptop.
:::

## Part 2: the writing {.smaller}

An updated draft of your midterm writing, same three sections:

- **Introduction**: the question, and why it matters
- **Methods**: the data, and what you did to it
- **Results**: including the results of a **statistical model**, not just plots

. . .

Figures should be better than the midterm's. You know ggplot2 now.

::: {.notes}
The upgrade from the midterm is the model. At midterm they were plotting; now
they fit something and report it.

Remind them that the text is theirs: the syllabus allows AI for code, not for
the writing in this section. That comes up again at the end of today.
:::

## Part 3: the presentation {.smaller}

About **five minutes**, during the final exam block.

A format that works:

- Title slide
- Background, 1 to 2 slides: what is your question, why does it matter
- Methods, 1 to 2 slides
- Results, 1 to 2 slides
- What you would do next

::: {.notes}
Five minutes is short. The commonest mistake is three slides of background and
no results.
:::

## Presenting well {.smaller}

- **Minimize text.** Roughly seven lines, seven words each, as an upper bound
- **Practice the timing**, out loud, with a clock
- **Going long costs points**, because it takes time from the next speaker

. . .

Your figures are the presentation. If a figure needs a paragraph of explanation,
fix the figure.

::: {.notes}
The 7x7 rule is a ceiling and not a target. Most good slides have less.

If anyone wants to go further on figures, the figures supplement covers
palettes, combining panels, and plotting model predictions.
:::

## Debugging {.center}

Something you have all been doing already.

## Get set up {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)

traits <- readRDS(url("https://tinyurl.com/amniotetraits"))

dim(traits)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
The amniote life-history database, about 21,000 species.

If readRDS complains, the usual cause is a missing url() wrapper: readRDS reads
a local file by default.
:::

## When something breaks {.smaller}

A workflow, roughly in order of effort:

1. **Re-read the code.** Most errors are typing
2. **Run it line by line** to find where it actually breaks
3. **Read the error message**, properly, all of it
4. **Search the error message**, with "R" and the package name
5. **Search a description** of what you are trying to do
6. Ask a person, with a **reprex**
7. Open an issue on the package's GitHub
8. Read the package's source and fix it yourself

::: {.notes}
Steps 1 to 3 solve most things and people skip them. The instinct to paste an
error into a search box, or now into a chatbot, before reading it is strong.

Steps 7 and 8 sound intimidating and are not. Package authors are usually
pleased someone cared enough to report a bug well.
:::

## The usual suspects {.smaller}

When the error is not obvious, check these before anything else:

- **Commas, quotes and parentheses.** Especially nested ones
- **Variable names.** `adult_svl` and `adult_svl_cm` are different columns
- **`NA`s**, which propagate silently through means and sums
- **Class.** A number read in as a factor behaves nothing like a number
- **Rows against columns.** `traits[4, ]` and `traits[, 4]` are very different

::: {.notes}
That last one catches people constantly and the error message never says
"you meant columns".
:::

## Your turn: four broken lines {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Each of these is broken **on purpose**. Run them, read the errors, fix them.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# all four of these are broken on purpose

# 1
traits |>
  group_by(class) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(adult_body_mass_g))

# 2
data.frame(scientific_name = paste(traits[4, ], traits[5, ]))

# 3
traits |>
  group_by(class) |>
  summarise(SD_svl = sd(adult_svl_cm))

# 4
traits >
  mutate(svl_mass_ratio = adult_svl_cm / adult_body_mass_g)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Ten minutes. Let them work before giving answers.

Note that 1 and 3 do not error at all, which is the point of including them.
:::

## What was wrong {.smaller}

| | Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | every mean is `NA` | `adult_body_mass_g` has 4,645 `NA`s; needs `na.rm = TRUE` |
| 2 | `"Aves Aves"` | `traits[4, ]` is **row** 4, not the genus column |
| 3 | every `sd` is `NA` | same `NA` problem, not a name problem |
| 4 | `object 'adult_svl_cm' not found` | `>` is not a pipe, so `mutate()` ran with no data |

. . .

**Three of the four never raised an error.** Code that runs is not code that
works, and that is the theme of the rest of today.

::: {.notes}
This is the hinge of the lecture. Set it up deliberately, because the AI section
at the end is the same lesson with higher stakes.

For 2, the fix is paste(traits$genus, traits$species).

Number 4 is the one to dwell on, because its error message actively misleads.
It names a column, so the instinct is to go hunting for a typo in the column
name. The column is fine. The bug is three characters earlier: `>` is not a
pipe, so mutate() was evaluated on its own, with no data attached, and the
column genuinely does not exist outside the data frame.

The lesson: an error message tells you where R gave up, not where you went
wrong.
:::

## Harder: errors inside loops {.smaller}

Debugging is harder inside `for()`, `while()` and `apply()`, because the thing
that breaks is on iteration 4,417 and you cannot see it.

Techniques:

- `message()` inside the loop, to print where you are
- Set `i` by hand and run the **body** line by line
- Re-run **only the iterations that failed**
- Have the loop record what it did, not just what it produced

::: {.notes}
The deepest habit to transmit: a loop that writes down what it is doing is
debuggable, and one that only returns a result is not.
:::

## A loop worth fixing {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# broken on purpose: run it, then work out why the answer is wrong
annual_fecundity <- NULL

for (i in 1:20) {
  species_i <- paste(traits$genus[i], traits$species[i])
  offspring_per_clutch <- traits$litter_or_clutch_size_n[i]
  clutches_per_year <- traits$litters_or_clutches_per_y[i]

  if (is.na(offspring_per_clutch) & is.na(clutches_per_year)) {
    next
  }

  out <- data.frame(species = species_i,
                    annual_offspring = offspring_per_clutch * clutches_per_year)

  annual_fecundity <- bind_rows(annual_fecundity, out)
}

annual_fecundity
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Two bugs, and neither raises an error.

The `&` should be `|`: as written, a species is skipped only when BOTH values
are missing, so rows with one missing value sail through and produce NA.

The loop also indexes traits by row while iterating over what the original code
called unique species, which is a mismatch worth pointing at. Here it is capped
at 20 rows to keep it quick.

Ask what the output would look like if you only ever checked that it ran.
:::

## Asking a person {.center}

## Search well {.smaller}

- Include **"R"** and the **package name**
- Paste the **error message**, but strip out your own object names
- If that fails, search a **description** of the goal rather than the error

. . .

Stack Overflow is quieter than it was, and more questions now go to chatbots
first. It is still the best archive of hard R problems that someone already
solved.

::: {.notes}
Honest framing rather than nostalgia. A lot of the value of Stack Overflow now
is as a corpus, including the corpus the chatbots learned from.
:::

## reprex {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

A **repr**oducible **ex**ample: the smallest complete thing that shows your
problem.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(reprex)

reprex({
  traits <- readRDS(url("https://tinyurl.com/amniotetraits"))
  traits |>
    ggplot(mapping = aes(x = adult_body_mass_g, y = adult_svl_cm)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_x_log10() +
    scale_y_log10()
})
```
:::

Run it and read the output.

::: {.notes}
It runs in a clean session, which is the whole point: it will fail on the
missing library(tidyverse) call, exactly as it would on a stranger's machine.

That is the lesson. Their code works because of things loaded hours ago that
they have forgotten about.
:::

## What makes an example reproducible {.smaller}

- It includes the `library()` calls
- It includes the **data**, or a few rows of it, or a link
- It is as **small** as possible while still breaking
- It is self-contained: no objects from your session

. . .

If your example is not reproducible, people may be unkind about it. If it is
reproducible, they may be unkind anyway, but you will usually get an answer.

::: {.notes}
Making a reprex solves the problem surprisingly often, because shrinking it to
the minimum is itself a diagnostic.
:::

## Asking for a favor {.smaller}

When you post a question or open an issue:

- **Be very nice.** You are asking a stranger to work for free
- Supply a reprex
- **Assume it is your error**, because it usually is
- Say what you already tried

. . .

For a package bug, open a **GitHub issue** on that package rather than posting
to a forum. That is where the person who can fix it reads.

::: {.notes}
"Assume it is your error" is both good manners and good odds.
:::

## AI and coding {.center}

## The landscape in 2026 {.smaller}

It is no longer one chatbot in a browser tab. Four different things, which
people all call "using AI":

| Mode | Examples | What arrives in your project |
|---|---|---|
| **Autocomplete** | Copilot in VS Code, RStudio, Positron | a few lines at a time, as you type |
| **Chat** | Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini | whatever you paste back |
| **Agent** | Claude Code, Copilot agent mode | files it edited and code it ran |
| **Review** | Copilot on a pull request | comments only, no code |

::: {.notes}
Worth naming these separately because the advice differs for each, and because
students will have used at least one without thinking of it as "AI".

Review is the safest: it only ever suggests. Agents are the most dangerous for a
beginner, because code enters the project without passing through your eyes.
:::

## What it is genuinely good at {.smaller}

- **Explaining an error message** you do not recognize
- **Translating between dialects**: base R to tidyverse and back
- **Boilerplate** you have written fifty times: themes, file loops, axis labels
- **Regular expressions**, which nobody enjoys
- Finding the **name of a function** you half-remember
- A first draft of **comments and documentation**

::: {.notes}
Notice what these have in common: in every case you can tell immediately whether
the answer is right, because you know what you wanted.
:::

## What it is bad at {.smaller}

- **Your data.** It has never seen it and will assume it is tidy and complete
- **Statistical judgment.** It will pick a model that matches the words in your
  question, not the structure of your data
- **Recent changes.** Packages move; training data has a cutoff
- **Saying "I don't know."** It will produce something either way

. . .

Hallucinated functions still happen, especially for small ecology packages, but
those are the **easy** failures: the code errors and you find out immediately.

::: {.notes}
Deliberately updating the older framing here. The current models invent fewer
functions than the 2023 ones did, and that improvement makes the remaining
failure mode more dangerous rather than less, because the obvious errors are
what used to make people check.
:::

## The failure that matters here {.smaller}

In a statistics course, the dangerous output is not code that breaks.

**It is code that runs, returns a plausible number, and is wrong.**

. . .

Debugging will never catch it. Nothing is broken. Only knowing the statistics
catches it, which is what this whole course has been for.

::: {.notes}
State this slowly. It is the single most important slide in the AI section and
it is the reason the earlier debugging exercise included two bugs that raised no
error.
:::

## A worked example {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Ask for "a test of whether bobwhite abundance declines with development" and you
can very reasonably get this:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
bw <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/class_examples/bobwhite_counts.csv")

model <- lm(count ~ frac_built, data = bw)

summary(model)
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(round(coef(summary(bad_fit)), 4))
```

Significant, negative, and it would pass any code review.

::: {.notes}
This is a real answer to a real question on real course data, and it is wrong.

Ask the room what they would write in a results section from that table. Someone
will say "abundance declines significantly with development, p < 0.001". That
sentence is what we are about to take apart.
:::

## Three checks you already know {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# 1. does it predict things that cannot exist?
predict(model, newdata = data.frame(frac_built = c(0, 0.5, 0.8)))

# 2. are the counts even close to normal? (Lecture 12)
var(bw$count) / mean(bw$count)

# 3. how much does it actually explain?
summary(model)$r.squared
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  check = c("predicted count at 50% developed",
            "predicted count at 80% developed",
            "variance / mean",
            "r squared"),
  value = c(round(predict(bad_fit, newdata = data.frame(frac_built = 0.5)), 2),
            round(predict(bad_fit, newdata = data.frame(frac_built = 0.8)), 2),
            round(var(bw$count) / mean(bw$count), 2),
            round(summary(bad_fit)$r.squared, 3))))
```

::: {.notes}
Every one of these is something they have done this semester.

Negative quail is the one that lands. The model is not slightly off, it is
describing an impossible world, for the same reason the straight line for
occupancy failed in Lecture 16: a line is unbounded and counts are not.

The variance to mean ratio of 10 says the spread is ten times what a Poisson
would give, so normal errors with constant variance are not close either.

And r squared of 0.04 means a highly significant result that explains four
percent of the variation. Significance is not effect size.
:::

## What it should have been {.smaller}

The model from Lecture 16: a negative binomial, with a mean that declines
exponentially so it can never go below zero.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.1
uu <- seq(0, 0.9, length.out = 200)
plot(bw$frac_built, bw$count, pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.12),
     xlim = c(0, 0.9), ylim = c(-15, 40),
     xlab = "fraction developed", ylab = "bobwhite counted")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey60", lty = 3)
lines(uu, coef(bad_fit)[1] + coef(bad_fit)[2] * uu, col = "#D81B60", lwd = 3)
lines(uu, nb_fit$par["mu0"] * exp(nb_fit$par["b"] * uu), col = "#1E88E5", lwd = 3)
legend("topright", c("lm: straight line", "negative binomial"),
       col = c("#D81B60", "#1E88E5"), lwd = 3, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

::: {.notes}
The pink line crosses zero at about 49% developed and keeps going. The blue one
approaches zero and never reaches it.

Worth saying: the AI was not stupid here. lm() is the right answer to a slightly
different question, asked about a different kind of data. It had no way to know
the response was an overdispersed count, because it never saw the data. You did.
:::

## How careful should you be? {.smaller}

It depends on what you are trying to learn.

. . .

**If you already know how to write it**, AI is a time saver, and you can review
what it gives you because you could have written it yourself.

. . .

**If you are still learning to write it**, writing it yourself *is* the
exercise. Skipping it means you will not be able to debug what you accepted, and
debugging is most of the job.

. . .

**Right now, in this course, you are mostly in the second group.** That is
deliberate, and it is temporary.

::: {.notes}
This is the honest version of the advice and it respects them.

The test to give them: could you have written this yourself, and can you explain
every line? If no to either, you have borrowed something you cannot maintain.

Say explicitly that this is not a permanent prohibition. Experienced people use
these tools heavily and review the output, which they can do because they spent
years learning what wrong code looks like.
:::

## What the course allows {.smaller}

From the syllabus, and it has not changed:

- **Code**: AI is allowed, on assignments, the midterm and the final project
- **Writing**: the text in your Part 1 and your final write-up is **yours**.
  No AI, no plagiarism
- **Any use must be cited**

. . .

If you are unsure whether something is permitted, ask. That is always cheaper
than the alternative.

::: {.notes}
Worth reading the policy out, because "cite it" is the part everyone forgets and
it is the part that turns a grey area into a non-issue.
:::

## How to cite it {.smaller}

Same principle as citing R and your packages. In your methods:

> Portions of the analysis code were drafted with [tool and version], then
> reviewed, tested and edited by the author.

. . .

And in the code itself, where it matters:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# first draft of this loop from Claude, checked against a manual
# calculation for the first three species
```

. . .

Many journals now require the same disclosure. You are practicing a real norm,
not a classroom one.

::: {.notes}
Pair this with the usual citation() reminder for R and packages, which they
already did for the midterm.

The in-code comment is the more useful habit of the two. Six months later it
tells you which parts you understood deeply and which you accepted on trust, and
that is exactly where bugs live.
:::

## Two things not to paste {.smaller}

- **Unpublished data** that is not yours to share, including a collaborator's or
  a lab's. A chat window is a third party
- **Anything under an agreement**: permits, embargoed data, human subjects data

. . .

Sending a few rows of a public dataset is fine. Uploading your advisor's
unpublished field data to a website is a conversation you do not want to have.

::: {.notes}
Short, practical, and it comes up in real labs.

If anyone asks about the energy and water cost of all this, or about models
being trained on other people's code without credit: both are real, both are
genuinely debated, and neither is settled. Worth naming rather than pretending
it is only a productivity question.
:::

## Your turn: break something {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

If you use an AI tool, ask it for an analysis you already know the answer to.

Suggestions, all from this course:

- "Fit a model of bobwhite counts against year"
- "Test whether reef fish richness differs with depth"
- "Is this distribution overdispersed?"

. . .

**Then check it the way we just did.** Does it predict impossible values? Does
the distribution match the data? Would you have written this?

::: {.notes}
Ten minutes if there is time, or sent home with them.

Asking for something they know the answer to is the point: it is the only way to
calibrate how much to trust the tool on something they do not.

Some will get a perfectly good answer, which is worth saying out loud. The goal
is calibration, not a demonstration that it always fails.
:::

## Take-away {.smaller}

1. **Read the error**, then run it line by line, then search it
2. **Code that runs is not code that works**
3. A **reprex** is how you ask a human, and it often answers itself
4. AI is good at things you can **check at a glance**, and unreliable at
   things that need to know your data
5. **Cite what you use**, including the tools

::: {.notes}
Point 2 is the one connecting the debugging half to the AI half, and it is worth
saying it is the same lesson twice.
:::
